stem: The price-index line shows a value of 102 in 2022 and 105 in 2023. What is approximately the inflation rate from 2022 to 2023?
explanation: Inflation is the percentage change in the price index: (105 - 102) / 102 × 100 ≈ 2.94%, which rounds to 2.9%.
choiceRationales: This reverses the direction of the price-index change; the index rose rather than fell.
The graph gives (105 - 102) / 102 × 100 ≈ 2.94%, so 2.9% is the appropriate rounded rate.
Five is the index-point change, not the percentage change using the earlier index as the denominator.
This overstates the change and does not follow from the two displayed index values.

stimulus.title: Price index over three years
stimulus.description: A line labelled P connects price-index values of 100 in 2021, 102 in 2022 and 105 in 2023.

stem: Which marked observation is below the displayed potential-output line while output is falling relative to the previous year?
choices: The observation labelled B, because it is the last observation and output is above potential.
The observation labelled A, because it is below potential and follows a higher output observation.
The observation labelled B, because it follows a lower observation and is therefore in decline.
Neither marked observation, because a below-potential observation alone cannot identify the position described.
explanation: A is below the horizontal Y* line and follows a higher output observation, so it is the marked observation with both properties.
choiceRationales: B is above the potential-output line, so this choice misreads the vertical position of the final observation.
A is below Y* and the output line falls from the preceding observation into A, so it satisfies both conditions.
B is not below Y*; it is above the reference line, so this confuses the direction of the output gap with the recent movement.
A satisfies both conditions. A single observation need not establish every feature of a full recession definition, but it does identify the graph position asked for here.

stimulus.title: Output relative to potential
stimulus.description: A line labelled Y records output from 2019 to 2024. A horizontal reference line labelled Y* is at 100. Points A and B are marked on the output line.

stem: Using GDP deflator = nominal GDP / real GDP × 100, what is the 2024 GDP deflator in the table?
choiceRationales: This does not use the 2024 nominal and real GDP values in the table.
This is too low because it understates the nominal-to-real ratio.
This is too high and is not the result of 286 divided by 250 times 100.
Dividing 286 by 250 and multiplying by 100 gives the displayed 2024 deflator of 114.4.

stimulus.caption: Nominal and real GDP
stimulus.note: Use the table values directly; the real-GDP measure uses the stated base year.

stem: At the wage floor shown in the labour-market graph, which conclusion follows?
choices: The floor is binding: labour supplied exceeds labour demanded, creating involuntary unemployment.
The floor is non-binding: the market remains at the unregulated equilibrium with no labour-market gap.
The labour-demand curve shifts right, so both employment and the real wage rise.
The labour-supply curve shifts left, so the equilibrium wage falls.
explanation: The wage floor is above the intersection of labour supply and demand. At that wage, workers want to supply more labour than firms want to hire.
choiceRationales: The floor lies above the equilibrium wage, so quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded and the difference is involuntary unemployment.
A floor above equilibrium is binding; the market does not remain at the unregulated intersection.
The graph shows a horizontal wage floor, not a rightward shift of labour demand.
The graph does not show a leftward supply shift, and that would not describe the displayed intervention.

stimulus.title: Labour market with a wage floor
stimulus.description: An upward-sloping labour-supply curve S and a downward-sloping labour-demand curve D intersect at E. A dashed horizontal line labelled w_f lies above E, with its intersections with the two curves marked L_D and L_S.

stem: The graph shows the labour-demand curve moving from D1 to D2 while labour supply is unchanged. Which interpretation is consistent with a permanent rise in worker productivity?
choices: A leftward shift of labour demand, lowering both the real wage and employment.
A rightward shift of labour demand, raising the equilibrium real wage and employment.
A movement down the unchanged labour-supply curve caused by a lower wage.
A rightward shift of labour supply, lowering the real wage while employment rises.
explanation: Higher productivity raises the value of marginal product of labour, shifting labour demand right. The displayed equilibria show higher employment and a higher real wage.
choiceRationales: The graph shows D2 to the right of D1, not a leftward shift.
A productivity increase raises labour demand; with supply fixed, the new equilibrium has higher employment and wage.
The movement is between two demand curves, so it is not a movement down the supply curve.
Labour supply is the unchanged curve in the graph, so it has not shifted right.

stimulus.title: Labour market equilibria
stimulus.description: An upward-sloping supply curve S is shown with two downward-sloping demand curves D1 and D2. D2 lies to the right of D1. Equilibria E1 and E2 are marked at the intersections of S with D1 and D2.

stem: Using unemployment rate = unemployed / labour force × 100, what is the unemployment rate in 2025?
explanation: The 2025 labour force is 920 + 80 = 1,000, so the unemployment rate is 80 / 1,000 × 100 = 8%.
choiceRationales: Ten percent is the 2024 rate, not the rate calculated from the 2025 row.
This uses an incorrect denominator or numerator for the 2025 labour force.
The 2025 labour force is 1,000 and 80 / 1,000 = 8%.
This incorrectly divides unemployment by employment rather than by the labour force.

stimulus.caption: Labour-market counts
stimulus.note: Counts are in thousands of people. The labour force is employed plus unemployed.

stem: Compared with E1, what happens at E2 when the saving curve shifts from S1 to S2 as shown?
choices: The real interest rate falls and equilibrium saving-investment quantity rises.
The real interest rate and equilibrium quantity both rise.
The real interest rate and equilibrium quantity are unchanged because investment is fixed.
The real interest rate rises while equilibrium saving-investment quantity falls.
explanation: The left/upward saving shift intersects the unchanged downward investment curve at a higher real interest rate and a lower quantity of saving and investment.
choiceRationales: The graph shows the new intersection at a higher, not lower, real interest rate and a lower quantity.
The real rate rises, but the horizontal coordinate moves left rather than right.
The saving shift changes the intersection even though the investment curve itself is unchanged.
At E2 the vertical coordinate is higher and the horizontal coordinate is lower, which is the crowding-out comparative static.

stimulus.title: Saving and investment equilibrium
stimulus.description: The graph has real interest rate on the vertical axis and saving or investment quantity on the horizontal axis. A downward-sloping investment curve I intersects two upward-sloping saving curves S1 and S2. S2 lies above and to the left of S1. Intersections E1 and E2 are marked.

xAxis.label: Saving and investment, S or I

topic: Investment demand and the real interest rate
stem: The horizontal line holds the real interest rate at r0 while investment demand moves from I1 to I2. What change is represented?
choices: Expected profitability has fallen or the user cost has risen, so planned investment is lower at the same r.
Household saving has shifted right, causing a movement along the unchanged investment curve.
The real interest rate has risen, causing a movement upward along I1.
Investment has risen because I2 lies below I1 at every quantity.
explanation: At the same real interest rate r0, the new investment curve gives a smaller planned investment quantity. That is a shift in investment demand, not a movement caused by a changed r.
choiceRationales: A lower demand curve means lower planned investment at the same real rate, consistent with lower expected returns or a higher user cost.
The graph contains two investment-demand curves and does not show a saving-curve shift.
The reference line fixes r at r0, so the change is not a movement caused by a higher real interest rate.
At the marked rate, I2 is to the left of I1, so the quantity of investment is lower, not higher.

stimulus.title: Investment and the real interest rate
stimulus.description: Two downward-sloping investment-demand curves I1 and I2 are shown, with I2 below and to the left of I1. A horizontal dashed reference line labelled r0 crosses both curves at points A and B.

stem: Using the approximation expected real rate = nominal rate − expected inflation, what is the expected real interest rate in 2026?
explanation: For 2026, the table gives a 5% nominal rate and 3% expected inflation, so the expected real rate is approximately 5% − 3% = 2%.
choiceRationales: One percent uses the realised inflation entry rather than expected inflation and also gives the wrong subtraction.
Subtracting the 3% expected inflation rate from the 5% nominal rate gives 2%.
Three percent is the expected inflation rate, not the expected real rate.
Eight percent adds the nominal rate and expected inflation rather than subtracting them.

stimulus.caption: Nominal rates and inflation
stimulus.note: All rates are annual percentages. Use expected inflation for the ex-ante calculation.

stem: The PAE curve shifts from PAE1 to PAE2. What happens to short-run equilibrium output?
choices: It rises from approximately 60 to approximately 80.
It falls from approximately 80 to approximately 60.
It stays at 45 because the 45-degree line determines autonomous spending.
It cannot be identified because the graph does not show a vertical price axis.
explanation: Equilibrium is where PAE intersects the 45-degree line. PAE1 intersects at about Y=60 and PAE2 at about Y=80.
choiceRationales: The two intersections with the 45-degree line are approximately (60,60) and (80,80), so equilibrium output rises.
This reverses the direction of the displayed PAE shift.
The 45-degree line represents Y=PAE; it does not fix autonomous spending at 45.
The income-expenditure diagram uses output and planned expenditure axes, so a price axis is not needed for this inference.

stimulus.title: PAE and the 45-degree line
stimulus.description: The graph shows a 45-degree line from the origin and two upward-sloping planned aggregate expenditure curves PAE1 and PAE2. PAE2 lies above PAE1. Equilibrium points E1 and E2 are marked at the two intersections with the 45-degree line.

stem: At the marked point A, what inventory movement and production response should occur?
choices: PAE is below Y, so unplanned inventories accumulate and firms reduce production.
PAE equals Y, so inventories and production are both unchanged.
PAE is above Y, so unplanned inventories fall and firms raise production.
PAE is above Y, so unplanned inventories rise and firms reduce production.
explanation: Point A lies above the 45-degree line, so planned expenditure exceeds current output. Firms sell more than they produce, inventories fall unexpectedly, and they respond by increasing production.
choiceRationales: A point below the 45-degree line would have PAE<Y, but A is above it.
A is not on the 45-degree line, so the income-expenditure equilibrium condition is not met.
The point is above the line, which means PAE>Y and the stated inventory and production responses follow.
When PAE>Y, inventories fall rather than rise; firms respond by raising production.

stimulus.title: Income-expenditure diagram
stimulus.description: A 45-degree line and an upward-sloping PAE curve are shown. The marked point A lies on the PAE curve at an output coordinate of 70 and a planned-expenditure coordinate of 82, above the 45-degree line.

stem: For scenario B, use k = 1 / (1 − c + m) to calculate the change in equilibrium output caused by the displayed autonomous-expenditure increase.
explanation: For B, k = 1/(1−0.8+0.2) = 2.5. Multiplying by the autonomous increase of 40 gives ΔY = 100.
choiceRationales: This does not apply the displayed multiplier parameters correctly.
The multiplier is 2.5 and 2.5 × 40 = 100.
This overstates the result relative to the 2.5 multiplier.
This treats the multiplier as four instead of 2.5.

stimulus.caption: Open-economy multiplier scenarios
stimulus.note: The multiplier is k = 1 / (1 − c + m).

topic: Fiscal expansion in the PAE model
stem: The graph shows a rise in government purchases shifting PAE0 to PAE1. Which statement best describes the new equilibrium?
choices: The 45-degree line shifts upward by the amount of the government-purchases change.
Output rises exactly one-for-one with government purchases in every three-sector model.
PAE shifts down and the equilibrium output falls because taxes must rise immediately.
PAE shifts up and equilibrium output rises by a multiplier effect, so the output change need not equal the initial spending change.
explanation: Government purchases are an autonomous component of PAE. Their increase shifts PAE upward and raises equilibrium output by the relevant fiscal multiplier rather than necessarily one-for-one.
choiceRationales: The 45-degree line represents the identity Y=PAE and does not shift when fiscal spending changes.
The multiplier generally makes the output response differ from the initial government-purchases change.
The displayed PAE shift is upward, and the question does not impose an immediate offsetting tax increase.
This matches the upward PAE shift and the multiplier mechanism in the three-sector model.

stimulus.title: Government purchases and PAE
stimulus.description: A 45-degree line and two upward-sloping planned aggregate expenditure curves PAE0 and PAE1 are shown. PAE1 lies above PAE0. Equilibrium points E0 and E1 are marked at the corresponding intersections with the 45-degree line.

stem: The graph shows a zero-primary-balance path with r greater than g. What does the displayed trajectory imply about the debt-to-GDP ratio?
choices: It is stable because the primary balance is zero.
It falls because GDP growth automatically cancels interest accumulation.
It rises over time because the interest-rate effect exceeds the growth effect.
It first falls and then becomes exactly zero.
explanation: When r>g, a zero primary balance is not enough to stabilise the debt ratio. The interest-rate effect causes the ratio to rise along the displayed path.
choiceRationales: A zero primary balance stabilises debt only under particular interest-growth conditions; r>g does not provide that condition.
The graph rises, and with r>g growth does not offset the interest effect.
The upward path is consistent with r>g and zero primary balance: the debt ratio increases.
Nothing in the graph shows a fall to zero; the displayed ratio increases throughout.

stimulus.title: Debt-to-GDP path when r exceeds g
stimulus.description: A line labelled b records the debt-to-GDP ratio over five periods. It starts at 60 and rises through 63, 66, 70 and 74. A dashed horizontal reference line labelled b0 is at 60. The text r > g appears near the upper-right of the graph.

stem: What is the 2025 debt-to-GDP ratio shown by the table?
explanation: The 2025 ratio is nominal government debt divided by nominal GDP: 900 / 2,250 × 100 = 40%.
choiceRationales: Dividing 900 by 2,250 and multiplying by 100 gives 40%.
This uses an incorrect denominator or does not apply the percentage conversion correctly.
This overstates the ratio relative to the table’s debt and GDP values.
This is not the result of the 2025 debt divided by 2025 GDP.

stimulus.caption: Government debt and GDP
stimulus.note: Calculate the ratio using debt divided by nominal GDP.

stem: Moving rightward along the bond-price curve from a low market yield to a high market yield, what happens to the price of the existing one-period bond?
choices: It rises because the bond’s fixed payment becomes more valuable.
It falls because the fixed payment is discounted at a higher yield.
It is unchanged because the face value is fixed.
It becomes equal to the market yield.
explanation: The present value of the fixed payment is lower when the market yield is higher, so the existing bond’s market price falls.
choiceRationales: A higher discount rate reduces rather than increases the present value of the fixed payment.
The curve slopes downward: a higher market yield corresponds to a lower price for the existing bond.
A fixed face value does not make the market price fixed before maturity.
Price and yield are distinct quantities with different units and are not equal.

stimulus.title: Existing bond price and market yield
stimulus.description: A downward-sloping curve labelled Pb relates the price of an existing one-period bond with a 100-dollar face payment to its market yield.

stem: With Y and P fixed, what does the arrow from A to B on the money-demand graph represent?
choices: A rightward shift of money demand caused by higher income.
A movement to higher real balances caused by a lower nominal interest rate.
A leftward shift of money demand caused by a lower price level.
A movement up and left along the same money-demand curve as the nominal interest rate rises, reducing real money demanded.
explanation: A to B moves along the same downward-sloping money-demand curve toward a higher interest rate and a lower real money balance. Y and P are held fixed, so this is not a curve shift.
choiceRationales: Income is held fixed and the graph shows movement along one curve rather than a rightward shift.
The arrow moves toward a higher interest rate and lower, not higher, real balances.
The price level is held fixed, and a price-level change would not be the displayed movement along the curve.
This matches the arrow and the inverse relationship between nominal interest rates and real money demanded at fixed Y and P.

stimulus.title: Money demand at fixed income and prices
stimulus.description: A downward-sloping curve labelled Md relates real money balances to the nominal interest rate. Points A and B lie on the curve, and an arrow points from A at (50,5) to B at approximately (35,7).

stem: What is Bank B’s reserve-deposit ratio using the balance-sheet data?
explanation: Bank B holds 75 million in reserves against 750 million in deposits, so the reserve-deposit ratio is 75/750 × 100 = 10%.
choiceRationales: This is below the ratio implied by 75 divided by 750.
This does not match the displayed reserves and deposits.
75 / 750 = 0.10, so the ratio is 10%.
This overstates the reserve share of Bank B’s deposits.

stimulus.caption: Selected commercial-bank balance-sheet data
stimulus.note: The reserve-deposit ratio is reserves divided by deposits.

topic: ES-balance demand and the cash rate
stem: The arrow moves along reserve demand from E1 to E2 as total ES balances increase. What happens to the overnight cash rate?
choices: It rises toward the lending ceiling.
It falls toward the deposit floor.
Reserve demand shifts right because the cash rate falls.
ES balances fall while the cash rate remains fixed at E1.
explanation: The reserve-demand curve slopes downward. Moving right to a larger quantity of ES balances corresponds to a lower overnight cash rate, closer to the floor.
choiceRationales: Moving right along the downward-sloping demand curve lowers rather than raises the rate.
E2 has more ES balances and a lower rate, toward the lower corridor boundary.
The arrow is a movement along reserve demand, not a rightward curve shift.
The arrow shows ES balances increasing from E1 to E2, not falling.

stimulus.title: Reserve demand inside the cash-rate corridor
stimulus.description: A downward-sloping reserve-demand curve Rd is shown between a dashed upper line labelled ceiling and a dashed lower line labelled floor. Points E1 and E2 lie on Rd, and an arrow points from E1 at (50,4) to E2 at (80,1.75).

stem: The policy reaction function shifts upward from PRF0 to PRF1. What does this mean at a fixed inflation rate for the real interest rate and policy stance?
choices: The central bank chooses a lower real interest rate and adopts a more expansionary stance.
The inflation rate must fall before the central bank changes its rate.
The economy moves along PRF0 because the inflation rate is unchanged.
The central bank chooses a higher real interest rate at every displayed inflation rate, adopting a more contractionary stance.
explanation: An upward exogenous shift of the course policy reaction function raises the policy-relevant real interest rate selected at any given inflation rate. That is a contractionary monetary-policy shift.
choiceRationales: An upward shift means a higher, not lower, selected real interest rate at the same inflation rate.
The graph describes a change in the rule, not a required prior movement in inflation.
The shift from PRF0 to PRF1 is not a movement along PRF0.
The vertical comparison at a common inflation rate shows a higher real interest rate under PRF1, which is contractionary.

stimulus.title: Policy reaction functions
stimulus.description: Two upward-sloping policy reaction functions PRF0 and PRF1 relate inflation to the real interest rate. PRF1 lies above PRF0. A dashed vertical line marks inflation of 4% and intersects both functions.

stem: According to the pension-payment row, what happens when the government pays households from its RBA account?
choices: Government-account balances fall, commercial-bank ES balances rise, and household deposits rise.
Government-account balances rise, ES balances fall, and household deposits fall.
Only household deposits change; total ES balances are unchanged.
ES balances fall because every government payment withdraws reserves from commercial banks.
explanation: A payment from the government’s RBA account transfers balances to commercial banks, increasing their ES balances and the recipients’ deposits while reducing the government account.
choiceRationales: This is the transaction shown: the government account is debited while the commercial-bank reserve account and household deposits are credited.
Those directions describe a tax payment rather than the pension payment row.
The table explicitly shows ES balances changing by +50 for the pension payment.
A payment from the government account adds, rather than withdraws, ES balances from commercial banks.

stimulus.caption: Stylised settlement effects of transactions
stimulus.note: Entries are changes in millions of dollars; a plus sign denotes an increase.

stem: The graph shows AD moving from AD0 to AD1. Which interpretation is consistent with a fall in autonomous exports?
choices: A movement up AD0 caused by higher inflation, with no change in autonomous spending.
A rightward shift of AD caused by stronger foreign demand for Australian output.
A leftward shift of AD, giving lower output at a given inflation rate.
A vertical shift of the potential-output line, leaving AD unchanged.
explanation: Lower autonomous exports reduce planned spending at each inflation rate, so the AD curve shifts left. At a common inflation rate, the displayed AD1 gives lower output than AD0.
choiceRationales: A movement along AD0 is associated with a change in inflation, not a change in autonomous exports.
A fall in exports reduces rather than increases autonomous demand; the graph shows AD1 to the left.
This matches the leftward shift and the lower output read at a common inflation rate.
The graph concerns the AD schedule; the potential-output line is not the shifted object.

stimulus.title: Aggregate-demand curves AD0 and AD1
stimulus.description: Two downward-sloping aggregate-demand curves AD0 and AD1 are shown, with AD1 to the left and below AD0. A horizontal dashed line marks a common inflation rate and intersects AD0 at A and AD1 at B.

stem: What economic change is represented by the shift from π0 to π1 in the graph?
choices: A favourable supply shock: inflation falls and output rises at the new short-run intersection.
A negative demand shock: inflation and output both fall along an unchanged SRAS curve.
A permanent fall in potential output, shown by a leftward movement of the AD curve.
An inflation-target increase that shifts the 45-degree line upward.
explanation: The graph uses the course's very-short-run convention: the short-run inflation line is horizontal at inherited inflation. The shift from π0 to the lower line π1 leaves the unchanged downward-sloping AD curve intersecting at lower inflation and higher output, which represents a favourable supply shock.
choiceRationales: The lower horizontal short-run inflation line, with unchanged AD, produces the displayed lower inflation and higher output.
A negative demand shock would move AD, not replace the horizontal short-run inflation line, and would lower output at a given inflation line.
A change in potential output would affect the potential-output reference, not create the lower inherited-inflation line shown here.
The 45-degree line is part of the PAE diagram, not this inflation-output diagram; the graph instead shows AD and short-run inflation lines.

stimulus.title: Short-run inflation-output diagram
stimulus.description: The graph has output on the horizontal axis and inflation on the vertical axis. A downward-sloping curve labelled AD crosses a horizontal line labelled π0 at E0 and a lower horizontal line labelled π1 at E1. E1 lies to the right of E0.

stem: Which row shows a negative output gap and therefore downward pressure on inflation when no adverse supply shock is present?
choices: Row B
Both rows
Neither row
Row A
explanation: Row A has Y below Y*: 98 compared with 100, giving a negative output gap. In the course’s short-run supply relation, that creates downward pressure on inflation absent an adverse supply shock.
choiceRationales: Row B has output above potential, so its output gap is positive rather than negative.
Only row A has Y below Y*; row B has Y above Y*.
The table contains one negative and one positive output gap, so at least one row qualifies.
Row A has (98−100)/100 = −2%, so it is the row with a negative gap.

stimulus.caption: Output relative to potential
stimulus.note: The output gap is (Y − Y*) / Y*.

stem: The graph shifts AUD demand from D0 to D1 while AUD supply is unchanged. Under the course convention e = USD/AUD, what happens?
choices: The AUD depreciates and e falls.
The AUD appreciates and e rises.
The exchange rate is unchanged because the graph is a flexible-rate market.
AUD supply shifts right, causing e to rise without a demand change.
explanation: The rightward AUD-demand shift raises the equilibrium price of an AUD in USD. With e measured in USD/AUD, a higher e is an AUD appreciation.
choiceRationales: A higher demand for AUD raises rather than lowers the USD price of an AUD.
The new equilibrium has a higher e, and under USD/AUD that is an appreciation of the AUD.
A flexible rate changes in response to the displayed demand shift.
The supply curve is unchanged; the graph explicitly shifts demand from D0 to D1.

stimulus.title: AUD demand and the exchange rate
stimulus.description: The vertical axis measures e in USD per AUD and the horizontal axis measures AUD quantity. An upward-sloping supply curve S intersects two downward-sloping demand curves D0 and D1. D1 lies to the right of D0. Equilibria E0 and E1 are marked.

topic: Defending an overvalued fixed exchange rate
stem: At the fixed rate shown, what imbalance exists and what intervention is required to defend the peg?
choices: Excess demand for AUD; the central bank sells AUD and accumulates foreign reserves.
Excess supply of AUD; the central bank sells AUD and accumulates foreign reserves.
Excess demand for AUD; the central bank buys AUD and runs down foreign reserves.
Excess supply of AUD; the central bank buys AUD and sells foreign reserves.
explanation: The fixed rate is above the flexible-market intersection, so AUD supplied exceeds AUD demanded. The central bank must buy the excess AUD, paying with foreign reserves.
choiceRationales: At a rate above equilibrium, the graph shows excess supply rather than excess demand for AUD.
The imbalance is correctly identified as excess supply, but selling AUD would add to that excess rather than absorb it.
Buying AUD is the correct intervention for excess supply, but it uses foreign reserves rather than describing excess demand.
The high peg creates excess AUD supply; buying AUD with foreign reserves is the displayed defence.

stimulus.title: AUD market with a fixed exchange rate
stimulus.description: The vertical axis measures e in USD per AUD. A downward-sloping AUD-demand curve D and an upward-sloping AUD-supply curve S intersect at e=0.60. A horizontal dashed fixed-rate line labelled e_bar is above the intersection at e=0.75.

stem: Using the two quotes in the table, approximately how many euros is one Australian dollar worth?
choices: €0.42 per AUD
€0.65 per AUD
€0.60 per AUD
€1.57 per AUD
explanation: One AUD is worth 0.65 USD, and each USD is worth 0.92 EUR. The cross-rate is 0.65 × 0.92 = 0.598 EUR/AUD, approximately €0.60 per AUD.
choiceRationales: This does not multiply the two displayed exchange rates and is too low for the cross-rate.
0.65 is USD per AUD, not euros per AUD; the USD-to-euro quote must also be applied.
Multiplying 0.65 USD/AUD by 0.92 EUR/USD gives approximately 0.60 EUR/AUD.
This is close to an inversion and does not use the quote directions as displayed.

stimulus.caption: Exchange-rate quotes
stimulus.note: Read each quote as units of the numerator currency per one unit of the denominator currency.

stem: Which statement is supported by the shape of the production function in the graph?
choices: The marginal product of capital diminishes as K rises, because the curve’s slope falls.
The marginal product of capital rises as K rises, because the curve is concave.
Output falls whenever capital rises, because the curve flattens.
Constant returns to scale require a straight production function in K alone.
explanation: The curve is increasing but concave: additional capital raises output while each additional unit adds less than the previous one. That is diminishing MPK.
choiceRationales: An increasing concave curve has a positive but declining slope, which is diminishing marginal product of capital.
Concavity means the slope falls, not rises, as capital increases.
The curve remains increasing, so output rises even though the increments become smaller.
Constant returns to scale is a joint property of scaling all inputs; this one-input graph does not require a straight line.

stimulus.title: Output and capital
stimulus.description: An increasing, concave curve labelled Y relates output to capital K. The curve passes through the displayed points (0,0), (20,45), (50,75) and (100,95).

topic: Capital deepening and output per worker
stem: Moving from A to B along the output-per-worker curve as capital per worker rises, what happens?
choices: Output per worker falls and the marginal gain becomes larger.
Output per worker is unchanged because only total capital matters.
Output per worker rises, but each additional unit of capital per worker adds less than the previous one.
Output per worker rises one-for-one with capital per worker because the production function has constant returns.
explanation: The curve rises from A to B but becomes flatter. Capital deepening raises output per worker while diminishing marginal returns make the additional gain smaller.
choiceRationales: The curve is upward sloping, so output per worker rises; its flattening means the marginal gain becomes smaller.
The graph directly relates output per worker to capital per worker, and the marked movement changes the former.
This describes the upward but concave curve and the movement from A to B.
Constant returns to scale does not imply a one-for-one relationship when capital per worker changes with other inputs held per worker.

stimulus.title: Output per worker and capital per worker
stimulus.description: An increasing, concave curve labelled y relates output per worker to capital per worker. Points A and B are marked at (25,40) and (60,65), with an arrow from A to B.

stem: For economy B, use ΔY/Y = ΔA/A + αΔK/K + (1−α)ΔL/L to calculate predicted output growth from the table.
choiceRationales: This underweights the capital contribution or omits part of the displayed calculation.
The TFP, capital and labour contributions sum to 2% + 1.8% + 0.7% = 4.5%.
This does not apply the α and 1−α weights to the two factor-growth rates correctly.
This overstates the weighted contributions and does not follow the growth-accounting identity.

stimulus.caption: Growth-accounting inputs
stimulus.note: All growth rates are percentages. The labour exponent is 1−α.
